sections.text:
The petty exactness of these men concerning syllables and words is not something simple, as one might suppose, nor does it tend toward some small evil. It contains a deep and concealed design against true religion. They are eager to prove that the expressions used of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are unlike, thinking that from this they will easily demonstrate a difference of nature.

They have an old sophism devised by Aetius, the champion of this heresy. Somewhere in one of his letters he wrote that things unlike in nature are expressed in unlike terms and, conversely, that things expressed in unlike terms are unlike in nature. As proof he dragged in the Apostle's words: “One God and Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” “As the expressions stand in relation to one another,” he says, “so also do the natures signified by them. ‘From whom’ is unlike ‘through whom’; therefore the Son is unlike the Father.”

The endless talk of these men about the expressions before us hangs upon this disease. To God the Father they assign, as though it were his exclusive inheritance, “from whom”; to God the Son they allot “through whom”; and to the Holy Spirit “in whom.” They say that the use of these expressions is never interchanged, so that, as I said, variation in wording may display variation in nature.

Yet they have not succeeded in hiding that by this hair-splitting over words they are trying to preserve the force of an impious argument. They want “from whom” to signify the Creator, “through whom” the subordinate minister or instrument, and “in whom” time or place, so that the Maker of all might be regarded as no more exalted than an instrument, and the Holy Spirit might appear to contribute to beings no more than the circumstance supplied by place or time.

translator_notes: Translated directly from Basil's Greek text in PG 32.
Basil is reporting the terminology of his opponents; he does not endorse their assignment of causal prepositions to the divine persons.
Aetius' linguistic argument is the immediate target of the chapter.
